transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-19
Start time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 min
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Diego (Redwood SE), Hannah (Redwood Solutions); Samir (Head of ML, IONYX), Leah (CTO), Ben (Platform Eng)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be incomplete):
IONYX is evaluating open model options for their customer support summarization + routing workflow. Primary concerns: context length for long chat histories (20k+ tokens), multilingual support (EN, ES, FR), tool-calling to hit internal search and internal DBs, and whether to run Hosted -> Dedicated -> Private as they scale. Security/regulatory constraints: EU data residency and internal audit trails. Next step is a pilot and sharing pricing/SOC2 materials.

Topics covered:
- model family tradeoffs (LLaMA variants, Mistral, Mixtral-like, commercial models)
- context window and memory/cache strategies
- multilingual hallucination risk and eval methodology
- tool-calling and function-calling: latency and connection patterns to internal search API
- deployment mode tradeoffs: Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private (VPC)

Action items (captured in metadata): Maya to send pricing/SLA, Diego to draft pilot/perf plan, Samir to share data samples.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining. i'm maya from Redwood, AE on this account. quick roll call?
[00:06] Samir: samir here, head of ml at ionyx. hey.
[00:08] Leah: leah here, im cto, quick on time.
[00:11] Ben: ben on platform team.
[00:13] Diego: diego from redwood se, i'll dig into perf stuff.
[00:16] Hannah: hannah from solutions, focus on onboarding and security.
[00:20] Maya: awesome. goal for today: understand your workload, context length, language needs and tool-calling requirements so we can recommend hosted vs dedicated vs private. also capture success criteria for a pilot. sound good?
[00:30] Leah: yep, that's perfect. to set context: we run a customer support product with long chat histories, doc attachments, and multi-lingual customers in eu and latam. primary use case is summarization + suggested routing, and some L2 automation via tools.
[00:45] Samir: budget conscious but we care latency below 700ms median for short requests, for longer chain-of-thought style summarizations we can tolerate up to 2s per token-ish, but overall cost matters.
[01:05] Diego: okay, nt. so when you say long chat histories, what's the typical token lengths you hit? any 1x outliers?
[01:12] Ben: most threads are between 2k and 6k tokens, but we see threads 18k to 22k when attachments are turned into text. we preprocess attachments into plaintext.
[01:28] Maya: cool. so context window is the big one. We support models with 16k, 32k, and up to 64k context sizes across various open families; for 20k ranges you want a 32k+ window or a prefixing/kvcache approach.
[01:46] Samir: yeah we looked at some stuff where you chunk + retrieval, but that adds complexity. can you run kv cache to stitch long histories without re-tokenizing every time?
[01:56] Diego: short answer: yes, our runtime supports KV-cache-friendly flows - we can do continuous caching of recent conversation and do prefix compression; for some models we also use selective truncation plus retrieval to keep high relevance. performance depends on model architecture and quantization.
[02:15] Leah: what about quantized models? we've seen docs where quantization reduces memory but increases hallucination for certain languages.
[02:24] Diego: correct tradeoff. 4-bit quant is great for cost and throughput on many open models (Llama2-family forks, Mistral variants), but lower precision can slightly degrade rare-token generation, which shows up in low-resource languages. We recommend a two-tier: eval with int8/qlora style first, then if quality unacceptable, fall back to 16-bit or hosted hardware with higher precision.
[02:46] Samir: ok. multilingual — which families have the best out-of-box for ES/FR? we've seen that LLaMA-derivative models sometimes struggle on idioms.
[02:56] Hannah: also want to know if Redwood offers eval baselines across languages.
[03:01] Maya: yes we have curated eval sets for en/es/fr and per-model baselines; we'll share a link. Practical note: Mistral-influenced models and bigger Llama variants tend to do better on western eu languages; for latin-american spanish you may still need domain tuning. we can run a small fine-tune or instruction-tune step during pilot.
[03:20] Ben: tool-calling: we need the model to call our internal search + a function that returns customer metadata. latency when calling external APIs is a concern. how does redwood handle function-calls?
[03:33] Diego: our function/tool-calling is built into the calling runtime. you can either proxy the calls via Redwood (hosted) or run the control plane with private connectors on VPC for private deployments. latency path: for hosted, the request flows to our runtime then out to your API endpoints if you whitelist them; for dedicated/private, it's direct in your VPC so network hops are shorter. we do streaming so you can start using partial outputs while tool calls are underway.
[04:00] Leah: what's the recommended pattern for low-latency lookups? synchronous function calls vs prefetched embeddings?
[04:08] Diego: if you can, maintain an embeddings index and prefetch top-k results; use tool-call for authoritative writes or complex db lookups. For 700ms median, prefetched embedding + cheap reranking is often safer.
[04:22] Samir: curious about caching — if we have repeated prefixes across chats, can we reuse KV cache to avoid recomputing?
[04:30] Diego: yes that's the KV prefix caching idea. we also do automatic prefix dedup and rolling snapshots — it reduces per-token compute but has higher memory footprint on GPUs. Dedicated pools can be configured with larger KV caches.
[04:44] Maya: switching to deployment modes: what's pushing you toward private or dedicated?
[04:50] Leah: primary drivers: eu data residency, auditability for enterprise customers, and ability to run in our VPC. We'd prefer private for the later stages; might start hosted to prototype.
[05:01] Maya: typical path: hosted for quick eval, dedicated reserved pools for scale and predictable latency, then private for compliance/regulatory. we can support pilot in hosted but with regional routing to eu to satisfy residency during evals.
[05:17] Ben: we have an internal security checklist — sso, audit logs, kms integration for keys. are those available for hosted?
[05:24] Hannah: we have SAML/SSO and audit logs available for all enterprise customers; for hosted we offer KMS integrations for token encryption and minimum retention options, but full dedicated KMS/HSM control is part of Private deployments. we'll attach the security onboarding doc.
[05:38] Leah: okay. what's the SLA on dedicated vs hosted?
[05:42] Maya: hosted has best-effort but SLA tiers exist on paid plans; Dedicated has SLA-backed uptime and latency targets. exact numbers I'll include in the pricing doc.
[05:52] Samir: let's talk about model choices — we want to avoid vendor lock and prefer open models but may evaluate some commercial ones for extreme latency/quality. What would you recommend to start with?
[06:05] Diego: for your workload i'd recommend starting with a 32k-window Mistral-like or a 70B Llama-derivative at 32k for summarization quality; run a parallel eval on a smaller distilled model for cheap reranking. So three tiers: small cheap model for quick runs, mid-size 32k model for production, big model as fallback for complex cases.
[06:26] Samir: do you support mixing model families in one runtime with routing? e.g., run 90% on efficient quantized model and 10% on bigger model for fallbacks.
[06:33] Diego: yes the smart routing layer supports percent-based routing, latency-based fallback and cost-based policies. you can pin routes to dedicated pools.
[06:42] Leah: what about eval metrics? we want to measure hallucination, rouge/bertscore for summarization, plus latency percentiles.
[06:51] Diego: we'll propose a pilot plan that includes a 1k-2k example prompt set, compute rouge/bertscore/qa-based faithfulness checks and track p50/p90/p99 latency plus cost per 1k tokens.
[07:06] Maya: quick tangent — are you constrained by budget cadence? procurement windows?
[07:11] Leah: q4 budget likely, but we can run a pilot before then. procurement will want SOC2 and SC docs.
[07:20] Ben: question on telemetry — can we get per-request token-level cost breakdowns?
[07:25] Hannah: yes Redwood Console exposes token-level and route-level breakdowns, tracing hooks and per-route dashboards; we can add custom tracing ids from your app to correlate.
[07:36] Samir: ok great. can we run an on-prem PoC if required? we have some air-gapped customers.
[07:42] Diego: yes, Private on-prem packages exist but take longer to onboard and typically require enterprise licensing; if you need air-gapped, we do an onsite installer path and integrate with your KMS/HSM.
[07:56] Leah: another risk - model updates breaking quality. do you support rollbacks and canarying?
[08:01] Maya: yes rollouts support canary, A/B, and automatic fallback policies if quality regressions are detected. we also link evaluation alerts to prompt sets so you can detect drift.
[08:12] Samir: i want to surface a subtle point: our legal team will ask about data retention and whether we can keep logs off-shore. how granular are retention policies?
[08:20] Hannah: you can set retention at route and org level; for private deployments you control retention entirely. For hosted, we have retention windows and the option to disable data collection on specific routes.
[08:32] Ben: about tool-calling security: is there a proxy mode where redwood never sees the PII payload? we prefer tokenized handles.
[08:40] Diego: you can use a transform layer where the model only sees anonymized IDs and the platform does a backend join to your systems in a secure function-call. For extremely sensitive data, private deployment is recommended.
[08:55] Samir: let's walk through a sample pilot outline. can you sketch timeline?
[09:00] Diego: sure: week 0: kickoff and data ingest (you provide 1-2k records). week 1: baseline eval across 3 model tiers and define metrics. week 2: latency runs and small scale dedicated run plus initial tool-call integration. by end of week 2 we have recommendation for production mode.
[09:18] Leah: that timeline seems aggressive but doable. procurement signoff may add a week.
[09:24] Maya: we'll send pricing and SLA, plus a security packet. we'll also include model baselines and our recommended preset configs for context caching and batch sizing.
[09:34] Samir: question on batching — will batching affect latency for interactive routes? we want to keep user-facing paths unbatched or carefully configured.
[09:44] Diego: yep, you can configure per-route batch windows and target latency. interactive routes typically use smaller batch sizes and prefer KV-cache so per-token latency is minimized. throughput-heavy async jobs can use larger batches for cost efficiency.
[09:58] Ben: any constraint on GPU types? we have preference for A100 vs H100 for our on-prem plans.
[10:05] Hannah: Dedicated pools have instance families choice; H100s are available for high-throughput/large context runs; A100 is supported and often used with quantized models. Private on-prem depends on customer infra.
[10:20] Leah: i'd like to see a concrete cost comparison: hosted per-token vs dedicated reserved monthly vs private licensing.
[10:26] Maya: we'll include a sample TCO sheet showing typical cost per 1M tokens across model tiers and deployment modes.
[10:33] Samir: anything we should prepare for the pilot?
[10:36] Diego: share - sample transcripts, expected QPS patterns, any GDPR-specific data flows, and the endpoints for tool-calls if you want us to do a network test.
[10:46] Samir: i'll share a redacted 1k sample set and a schema of our tool-call endpoints.
[10:51] Leah: ok thanks, what are immediate next steps?
[10:54] Maya: i'll email pricing/SLA and security packet today; Diego will send pilot plan by monday; Samir to share data by sunday. we'll target kickoff the following week.
[11:05] Ben: sounds good.
[11:07] Maya: great thanks everyone. we'll follow up with a calendar invite for kickoff.
[11:12] Leah: thanks all.
